sections.heading: Overshoot from slow voltage loop
sections.text: Push-pull overshoot is usually from a slow voltage loop that cannot handle the load step fast enough. If using voltage-mode control, switch to peak-current-mode for faster response and inherent flux balancing.

sections.heading: Slow settling
sections.text: If the push-pull settles slowly, check: (1) Is the current loop fast enough? f_ci should be fsw/5 or higher. (2) Is slope compensation too aggressive? Excessive ramp reduces the current-loop gain. (3) Is the transformer saturating from flux imbalance?

sections.heading: Excess ripple from leakage inductance
sections.text: Push-pull output ripple can be dominated by the leakage-inductance ring with MOSFET output capacitance. Add an RCD snubber across each primary half-winding. The snubber voltage should be 2-3x V_in.

sections.heading: Efficiency from transformer losses
sections.text: Push-pull efficiency is dominated by transformer copper/core losses and switch conduction losses. The controller cannot improve efficiency. Consider: better core material, larger wire gauge, synchronous rectification on the secondary.

sections.heading: Flux imbalance
sections.text: If the push-pull shows core saturation (rising current, collapsing output), the flux balance is broken. Verify: per-switch current sensing, symmetric gate drive, D<0.5. If flux imbalance persists, add a small air gap to the transformer core or use current-mode control with per-switch sensing.
